svg.aria-label: Diagram: Amazon EBS now supports associating additional KMS keys with encrypted snapshots. An associated KMS key is an additional customer managed key, and a principal with access to it can access the snapshot's data for cross-account sharing and copying without being granted access to the existing KMS key that encrypts the snapshot. The associated key does not replace or change the existing key, does not grant access to it, and associating it does not re-encrypt the snapshot's data, so the separation is between access to the data and access to the key that encrypts the data. The case this genuinely unblocks is the AWS managed key: a snapshot encrypted under one cannot be shared with or copied to another account at all, because an AWS managed key's key policy cannot be modified to grant access to another account, so the only previous remedy was a full copy into a customer managed key before sharing. Cross-account use requires two separate grants and granting one without the other is not sufficient: the associated key's key policy must allow the other account's principal to use the key, and that principal's IAM policy in their own account must also allow them to use it. The limits are that you can associate a key only with an encrypted snapshot, the associated key must be a customer managed key and cannot be an AWS managed key, you cannot associate a key the snapshot already uses, you cannot associate a key with a snapshot in the Archive tier, and to create a volume from an encrypted snapshot you must have access to the existing KMS key, which means the recipient's path is a copy under the associated key rather than a direct restore, moving the re-encryption from two copies to one. Operations are associate-kms-key-id and disassociate-kms-key-id with the AssociatedKmsKeys field on describe-snapshots, and the permissions are ec2:AssociateKmsKeyId and ec2:DisassociateKmsKeyId plus the KMS permissions EBS requires. Authorization failures name the key you are not authorised to use.
svg.title: An associated key grants the data, not the key that encrypts it
svg.text: Access to the data, separated from access to the key that encrypts it.
“The associated KMS key does not replace or change the existing KMS key that encrypts the snapshot, it does
not grant access to that key, and associating it does not re-encrypt the snapshot’s data.”
The case it unblocks rather than merely speeds up
“If the snapshot is encrypted under an AWS managed key, you can’t share it with or copy it to another
account, because an AWS managed key’s key policy can’t be modified to grant access to another account.”
A hard stop, not a slow path. The old remedy was copying every gigabyte into a CMK first.
WHAT AN ASSOCIATED KEY GRANTS
Cross-account share of the snapshot
Copy by the receiving account
Removable later: disassociate-kms-key-id
Visible only in the AssociatedKmsKeys field.
WHAT IT DOES NOT GRANT
Creating a volume from the snapshot
— that still needs “the existing KMS key”.
So the recipient copies first, then restores
from their own copy.
The re-encryption did not vanish — it moved
before: owner copies into a CMK + recipient copies into their own key = 2 copies
now: owner associates a key (metadata) + recipient copies = 1 copy
Two grants, in two accounts, and one alone does nothing
The key policy must allow the other account’s principal. That principal’s own IAM policy must allow the key.
“Granting one without the other is not sufficient.” Authorization errors name the key — read them first.
Limits: encrypted snapshots only · the associated key must be customer managed · not a key the snapshot
already uses · and not a snapshot in the Archive tier — which is where long-retention copies live.
An association is a standing second door to the data, and the encrypting key’s policy will never mention it.
If your answer to “who can read this snapshot” comes from key policies alone, it is now incomplete.
